case_notes:
Provisional diagnosis: MDS.

74F, macrocytic anaemia, Hb 92 g/L, no transfusion requirement yet. Neutrophils and platelets normal. Marrow: hypercellular, erythroid dysplasia with ring sideroblasts, no excess of blasts. Karyotype normal.

NGS:
- SF3B1 p.(Lys700Glu), VAF 38%
- TET2 p.(Gln1548Ter), VAF 22%
- ASXL1 p.(Gly646TrpfsTer12), VAF 9%

## Negative-result semantics

When the patient NGS result is explicitly complete, a listed panel gene that is absent from the detected-variant list is interpreted as **no SNV, short insertion/deletion, or short-range complex variant detected in that gene within the validated assay scope**.

Use this negative result when applying diagnostic, prognostic, biomarker, treatment, germline, and other reporting rules. Do not treat the gene as unresolved merely because it is not individually listed in the patient result.

This inference is limited to the assay scope. It does not establish whole-gene biological wild type and does not exclude copy-number changes, rearrangements, structural variants, or other variant classes unless the patient result or another supplied test explicitly assesses them.

If the patient NGS result is described as partial, selected, limited, abbreviated, pending, or otherwise incomplete, do not infer a negative result for an unlisted panel gene.

diagnosis_evidence_cards.interpretation: In suspected primary myelofibrosis, detection of ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, or TET2 mutation can support the clonal nature of disease when canonical MPN-driver mutations are absent.
In myeloproliferative neoplasm, unclassifiable (MPN-U), ASXL1, EZH2, IDH1, IDH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, or TET2 mutations detected by sensitive molecular methods can support the clonal nature of disease.

According to the ICC, atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML) requires WBC >=13 x 10^9/L due to neutrophils and precursors with promyelocytes/myelocytes/metamyelocytes >=10%; cytopenia using MDS thresholds; <20% blasts; prominent dysgranulopoiesis; monocytes <10% and eosinophils <10% of leukocytes; hypercellular marrow with granulocytic proliferation/dysplasia; and absence of BCR::ABL1 and TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms. Absence of JAK2, CALR, and MPL supports the diagnosis, and SETBP1 mutation, often with ASXL1, provides additional support.

According to the ICC, MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis requires thrombocytosis >=450 x 10^9/L and anemia present at initial diagnosis, <1% blood blasts and <5% marrow blasts, and SF3B1 mutation with VAF >10%; no recent cytotoxic/growth-factor therapy explaining the phenotype; no prior MPN, MDS, or other MDS/MPN; and absence of BCR::ABL1, TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms, t(3;3), inv(3), and del(5q) meeting MDS-del(5q) criteria. Ring sideroblasts are not required when SF3B1 VAF is >10%; JAK2 V617F, CALR, or MPL W515 co-mutation is not required but supports the diagnosis.

According to the ICC, MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis, NOS requires thrombocytosis >=450 x 10^9/L and anemia present at initial diagnosis, erythroid dysplasia with >=15% ring sideroblasts, <1% blood blasts and <5% marrow blasts, and clonality by cytogenetic abnormality and/or somatic mutation (or, if clonality is absent, no recent cytotoxic/growth-factor therapy explaining the phenotype); no prior MPN, MDS, or other MDS/MPN; and absence of SF3B1 mutation, BCR::ABL1, TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms, t(3;3), inv(3), and del(5q) meeting MDS-del(5q) criteria.
MDS with SF3B1 mutation that later develops thrombocytosis is classified as thrombocytotic progression of MDS-SF3B1 rather than MDS/MPN with thrombocytosis.

For clonal cytopenias spanning CCUS to MDS, the ICC defines cytopenia as acquired sustained hemoglobin <12 g/dL in females or <13 g/dL in males, ANC <1.8 x 10^9/L, and/or platelets <150 x 10^9/L not explained by another condition.
VEXAS syndrome is associated with somatic UBA1 mutation and should be kept separate from MDS unless morphologic MDS criteria are met.

According to the ICC, MDS is a clonal hematopoietic neoplasm defined by persistent unexplained cytopenia and morphologic dysplasia, generally chronic for about >=4 months and not explained by drug, toxin, or comorbidity; a 10% dysplasia threshold is recommended for each lineage, and demonstrable clonality is not required when qualifying dysplasia and cytopenia are present. BCR::ABL1 or a TK-fusion myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm excludes MDS. At initial diagnosis, persistent WBC >=13 x 10^9/L, platelets >=450 x 10^9/L (except MDS-del(5q) or inv(3)/t(3;3)), or monocytes >=0.5 x 10^9/L and >=10% of leukocytes instead favors MDS/MPN or MPN classification.

According to the ICC, MDS with mutated SF3B1 requires SF3B1 mutation VAF >=10%, at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis at diagnosis, <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and absence of multihit TP53, RUNX1 mutation, isolated del(5q), -7/del(7q), 3q26.2 abnormalities, and complex karyotype. Dysplasia is typically present but is not required, and ring sideroblasts are not required.
SF3B1-unmutated MDS with ring sideroblasts is classified as MDS, NOS irrespective of ring-sideroblast number.
In cytopenic patients lacking dysplasia, prior MDS-defining cytogenetic abnormalities other than del(5q), -7/del(7q), or complex karyotype are now classified as CCUS rather than MDS.

According to the ICC, MDS with excess blasts requires at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis, and 5%-9% marrow blasts or 2%-9% blood blasts; 1% peripheral-blood blasts confirmed on two occasions also qualifies. Dysplasia is typically present but not required, multihit TP53 is excluded in favor of MDS with mutated TP53, and excess blasts supersede other non-TP53 MDS subtypes. In patients <18 years, MDS with excess blasts uses 5%-19% marrow blasts and 2%-19% blood blasts, and MDS/AML does not apply.

According to the ICC, MDS with del(5q) requires at least one cytopenia, del(5q) isolated or with no more than one additional cytogenetic abnormality other than -7/del(7q), <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and absence of multihit TP53. Thrombocytosis is allowed but other ICC-defined cytoses are not; dysplasia is typically present but is not required.

According to the ICC, MDS, NOS without dysplasia requires at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis, <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and -7/del(7q) or complex karyotype as the defining cytogenetic abnormality; multihit TP53 and SF3B1 mutation with VAF >=10% are excluded.

According to the ICC, MDS, NOS with single-lineage dysplasia requires dysplasia in one lineage, at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis, <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and failure to meet criteria for MDS with del(5q) or MDS with mutated SF3B1; multihit TP53 is excluded.

According to the ICC, MDS, NOS with multilineage dysplasia requires dysplasia in at least two lineages, at least one cytopenia, no ICC-defined cytosis, <5% marrow blasts and <2% blood blasts, and failure to meet criteria for MDS with del(5q) or MDS with mutated SF3B1; multihit TP53 is excluded.

According to the ICC, MDS with mutated TP53 has 0%-9% blasts and requires multihit TP53, defined as 2 distinct TP53 mutations each with VAF >10% or one TP53 mutation plus 17p deletion, VAF >50%, or copy-neutral LOH at TP53; when LOH information is unavailable, TP53 mutation VAF >10% with complex karyotype qualifies. Complex karyotype without a TP53 mutation does not qualify, and monoallelic TP53-mutated MDS is excluded from this entity.
Established MDS that acquires a TP53 mutation can be redesignated as MDS, MDS/AML, or AML with mutated TP53 according to blast count.

Development of leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, or monocytosis during established MDS generally does not warrant reclassification as MDS/MPN; the disease can instead be designated as MDS with neutrophilic, thrombocytotic, or monocytic progression.
The ICC recommends retaining the morphologic/genetic MDS diagnosis as primary and adding a therapy-related qualifier when disease follows cytotoxic therapy.
The ICC recommends qualifying CHIP, CCUS, and other non-MDS clonal cytopenias as therapy-related when they follow marrow exposure to chemotherapy or radiation.
Any underlying germline predisposition mutation or syndrome should be specified as a qualifier after the MDS diagnosis and subtype.
In germline RUNX1-, ANKRD26-, or ETV6-associated constitutional platelet disorders, marrow megakaryocytic dysplasia can be present with isolated thrombocytopenia in the absence of MDS.
When assessing MDS in patients with germline predisposition, baseline dyspoietic bone-marrow changes can be present even in the absence of a myeloid malignancy.

In patients with germline predisposition, development of MDS is generally associated with new or progressive cytopenia, often with rising marrow cellularity, overt multilineage dysplasia, increased blasts, and/or acquired pathogenic genetic abnormalities.
In a patient with germline predisposition, emergence of del(5q), -7/del(7q), complex karyotype, multihit TP53 mutation VAF >10%, or SF3B1 mutation VAF >10% is considered MDS-defining.
In Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, a small stable clone with monoallelic TP53 mutation alone is not considered MDS, whereas biallelic TP53 mutation is associated with myeloid malignancy.
According to the ICC, MDS/AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations has 10%-19% blasts and is defined by mutation in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2.
According to the ICC, AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations requires >=20% blasts and is defined by mutation in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2.

For TP53-mutated MDS, a single TP53 mutation with a retained wild-type copy represents a monoallelic state, whereas multiple TP53 mutations or TP53 mutation(s) with TP53 deletion or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity represent multi-hit TP53, consistent with biallelic targeting.
diagnosis_evidence_cards.paper_nickname: Bernard TP53 Allelic State in MDS 2020

diagnosis_evidence_cards.interpretation: Under the 2022 ICC, when higher-priority recurrent AML-defining abnormalities and TP53-mutated disease are absent, pathogenic mutations in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, RUNX1, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2 define AML with myelodysplasia-related gene mutations at ≥20% blasts, irrespective of prior MDS; the corresponding 10%-19% blast category is MDS/AML.
Under the 2022 ICC, a prior MDS is appended as a diagnostic qualifier to the AML category only when it was established by standard diagnostics more than 3 months before AML diagnosis.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, cytopenia thresholds harmonized across CCUS, MDS and MDS/MPN are haemoglobin <13 g/dL in males or <12 g/dL in females, absolute neutrophil count <1.8 × 10^9/L, and platelets <150 × 10^9/L.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, the term “myelodysplastic neoplasms,” abbreviated MDS, replaces “myelodysplastic syndromes.” MDS is defined as a clonal haematopoietic neoplasm with cytopenia(s) and morphologic dysplasia, with a recommended dysplasia threshold of ≥10% in a lineage.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with low blasts and isolated 5q deletion requires <5% bone-marrow blasts and <2% peripheral-blood blasts, with 5q deletion alone or with one additional abnormality other than monosomy 7 or 7q deletion. An SF3B1 mutation or a TP53 mutation that is not multi-hit does not by itself override the MDS-5q diagnosis.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with low blasts and SF3B1 mutation is a genetically defined MDS type in which 5q deletion, monosomy 7 and complex karyotype are exclusionary. Detection of ≥15% ring sideroblasts may substitute for an SF3B1 mutation; for SF3B1-wild-type cases with ≥15% ring sideroblasts, “MDS with low blasts and ring sideroblasts” is an acceptable alternative term.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation requires <20% blasts in blood and marrow plus either ≥2 TP53 mutations or one TP53 mutation with TP53 copy-number loss or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity. Two or more TP53 mutations can generally be considered multi-hit status. MDS-biTP53 supersedes MDS-5q and MDS-SF3B1 in the WHO5 genetic hierarchy.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, hypoplastic MDS is a distinct MDS type defined by bone-marrow cellularity ≤25%, adjusted for age.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, distinction between single-lineage and multilineage dysplasia is optional rather than disease-type defining in MDS.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, a 20% blast cutoff is retained to delineate MDS from AML, but most AML types with defining genetic abnormalities may be diagnosed below 20% blasts. AML with BCR::ABL1 and AML with CEBPA mutation remain exceptions requiring ≥20% blasts. When a genetically defined AML is diagnosed below 20%, morphologic and molecular findings must be correlated to establish that the defining abnormality is driving the disease.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, childhood MDS with low blasts replaces the former term refractory cytopenia of childhood and is defined by <5% bone-marrow blasts and <2% peripheral-blood blasts. It comprises hypocellular and NOS subtypes, and diagnosis requires exclusion of non-neoplastic causes of cytopenia, bone-marrow failure syndromes and germline pathogenic variants.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, childhood MDS with increased blasts is defined by 5–19% bone-marrow blasts or 2–19% peripheral-blood blasts.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis is redefined on the basis of SF3B1 mutation and renamed MDS/MPN with SF3B1 mutation and thrombocytosis. For SF3B1-wild-type cases with ≥15% ring sideroblasts, MDS/MPN with ring sideroblasts and thrombocytosis remains acceptable terminology.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, AML, myelodysplasia-related (AML-MR; formerly AML with myelodysplasia-related changes) requires ≥20% blasts with a myeloid immunophenotype plus at least one qualifying MDS-related feature: a history of MDS or MDS/MPN; a defining somatic mutation in ASXL1, BCOR, EZH2, SF3B1, SRSF2, STAG2, U2AF1 or ZRSR2; or a defining cytogenetic abnormality comprising complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities), 5q deletion/loss, monosomy 7 or 7q deletion/loss, 11q deletion, 12p deletion/loss, monosomy 13 or 13q deletion, 17p deletion/loss, isochromosome 17q or idic(X)(q13). Morphologic dysplasia alone is insufficient. A diagnosis of acute erythroid leukaemia supersedes AML-MR.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, a myeloid neoplasm post cytotoxic therapy (MN-pCT) is diagnosed when criteria for AML, MDS or MDS/MPN are fulfilled in a patient with a documented history of chemotherapy or large-field radiation therapy for an unrelated neoplasm. CCUS is excluded. NPM1-mutated disease and core-binding-factor leukaemias with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 or CBFB::MYH11 still receive the post-cytotoxic designation when the exposure history is present. PARP1 inhibitors qualify as an exposure and methotrexate does not. The specific myeloid diagnosis should be given when possible with “post cytotoxic therapy” appended.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with low blasts is defined by <5% bone-marrow blasts and <2% peripheral-blood blasts.

According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with increased blasts is subgrouped as MDS-IB1, defined by 5–9% bone-marrow blasts or 2–4% peripheral-blood blasts, and MDS-IB2, defined by 10–19% bone-marrow blasts, 5–19% peripheral-blood blasts, or Auer rods.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS with fibrosis has 5–19% bone-marrow blasts and 2–19% peripheral-blood blasts.
According to WHO 5th Edition 2022, MDS, unclassifiable is no longer a recognized MDS category.
In unexplained cytopenia, SF3B1 mutation strongly supports an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, including when SF3B1 is the only detected mutation.
In unexplained cytopenia, SRSF2, U2AF1, ZRSR2, JAK2, or RUNX1 mutation strongly supports an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, whether detected alone or with other mutations.

In unexplained cytopenia, an isolated TET2, DNMT3A, or ASXL1 mutation provides substantially less support for an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, than the same mutation occurring with additional genetic lesions.
In unexplained cytopenia, TP53 mutation is more supportive of an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype, when co-mutated—most often with TET2 or ASXL1—than when TP53 is isolated.

In unexplained cytopenia, co-mutation patterns in which TET2, DNMT3A, or ASXL1 co-occurs with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, TP53, NRAS, CUX1, or IDH2 are highly predictive of an underlying myeloid neoplasm, unspecified by subtype.

In unexplained cytopenia, SF3B1 mutation is highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes—even when SF3B1 is the only detected mutation.
In unexplained cytopenia, ZRSR2 mutation is highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes.

In unexplained cytopenia, co-mutation patterns in which TET2, ASXL1, or DNMT3A co-occurs with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, BCOR, CUX1, TP53, IDH1, or IDH2 are highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes.

In unexplained cytopenia, SRSF2 or U2AF1 mutation is highly specific for a myeloid neoplasm with myelodysplasia—MDS, MDS/MPN, or AML with myelodysplasia-related changes—except when co-occurring with JAK2 in primary myelofibrosis.

In patients with CCUS and inconclusive dysplasia, the authors propose that highly specific mutation patterns—SF3B1, SRSF2, U2AF1, or ZRSR2 mutation, or TET2, ASXL1, or DNMT3A co-mutated with RUNX1, EZH2, CBL, BCOR, CUX1, TP53, IDH1, or IDH2—may provide presumptive evidence of MDS even when definitive morphologic criteria are absent.
In MDS with del(5q), del(5q) can be the sole founding and disease-defining genetic lesion; an accompanying sequence mutation is not required.

In TP53-mutated AML/MDS, findings supporting multihit TP53 status include TP53 cnLOH demonstrated by dedicated testing; loss of chromosome 17 or 17p; two or more TP53 mutations; or a single TP53 mutation with VAF >55% and sequencing coverage >200×. A TP53 VAF <55% does not exclude multihit disease.

In TP53-mutated AML/MDS, complex karyotype may suggest multihit TP53 status but is an imperfect surrogate: some TP53-mutated cases with complex karyotype lack chromosome 17 deletion or TP53 cnLOH, whereas some cases with TP53 cnLOH have noncomplex karyotypes.

According to WHO 2022 as summarized by Urrutia et al., MDS with biallelic TP53 inactivation has <20% blasts and no history of cytotoxic or radiation therapy; biallelic TP53 inactivation is defined by two or more TP53 mutations, one TP53 mutation with chromosome 17/17p copy loss, or one TP53 mutation with TP53 cnLOH.
